yarn-troppo.meaning: Every beat is there in order, from the apprentices to the ash-barrel, with the forecast and postscript kept word for word. It adds asides that hang off the original: "Not a word of a lie.", "Weather coming out his ears, basically.", "Bit late to ask now.", "Hedging his bets, the poor fella." and "Cleaned the place out." The last one spells out the Congressman joke rather than adding a fact. "I grabbed him" is a small invented action.
yarn-troppo.sense: The terms fit: "blow-ins" for casual visitors, "brolly" for umbrella, "a pollie had been through" for the Congressman, "knocked the foreigners for six" for astounded, "do in a fair few poets" for kill. "patient, easygoing types" is a little softer than forbearing, but it holds.
yarn-troppo.authenticity: Mostly natural spoken Aussie: "my money's on a mob of raw apprentices", "take their custom down the road", "never knocking off", "proud as punch". A few lines are stock, like "scratches his noggin" and "But what can ya do?", and the opener "Now, ya might've heard this one." is bolted on.
yarn-troppo.register: This is heavier than level 2. It retells the whole piece as a yarn, with an added opener ("Now, ya might've heard this one."), repeated exclamations ("A hundred and thirty-six!", "Four days!") and tags like "Weather coming out his ears, basically." It reads closer to level 3 or 4. There's no swearing, which fits vulgarity 0.
yarn-troppo.tone: The deadpan tall tale survives, but the added punchlines sometimes explain the joke: "a pollie had been through. Cleaned the place out." undercuts the dry aposiopesis, and "Covers the lot, doesn't it?" nudges the reader. The comic grandeur is still there in "Down the cellar with his head in the ash-barrel, that's where."
yarn-troppo.flow: It reads well aloud, with good paragraphing and rhythm: "Variety? He owned up he'd got hundreds of kinds of weather he'd never even heard of. Quantity? Well...". Some of the short added fragments ("Four days!", "Not a clue what New England's going to do.") get choppy.
yarn-troppo.variety: The slang is varied ("mob", "blow-ins", "brolly", "pollie", "knocked the foreigners for six", "proud as punch", "Strewth"), and the openers and tags differ from one to the next.
yarn-troppo.essence: It is unmistakably Twain's weather speech: the apprentices, the Centennial collector, the murdered poets, Old Probabilities' forecast and the thunder concert, all retold. The extra explaining dents the deadpan a little.

yarn-deadset.meaning: It follows the original sentence by sentence and loses nothing; "a pollie had been there" localises the Congressman. "who muck about and learn how" makes experiment slightly sloppier, but the sense holds.
yarn-deadset.sense: The terms fit: "gobsmacked the foreigners", "blow-ins", "brolly", "spot-on prophecy", "chucked all that was blemished", "big letdowns". "muck about" for experiment implies aimlessness, a slight strain.
yarn-deadset.authenticity: The swaps are natural Aussie ("I dunno who makes that, but I reckon", "blow-ins", "Strewth, what awful thunder you've got here!"), but they sit inside Twain's untouched formal syntax: "I reverently believe", "you stand from under", "by and by he comes out with". The mix sometimes reads as patched.
yarn-deadset.register: A light, steady touch about right for level 2: "dunno", "reckon", "bloke", "gobsmacked", "blow-ins", "heaps", "brolly", "pollie", "Strewth". There's no swearing.
yarn-deadset.tone: The dry, mock-solemn humour comes through whole, because the structure and punchlines are Twain's own: "you'd think it was something valuable, and a pollie had been there."
yarn-deadset.flow: It is one long unbroken block like the original. The joins are mostly smooth, but some mixed lines clunk: "I reverently believe" beside "I dunno", and "It was me that made the fame and fortune of that bloke that had that marvellous collection".
yarn-deadset.variety: The swaps are varied and nothing repeats; "reckon" appears only once or twice.
yarn-deadset.essence: It is plainly the original with a light Aussie accent, and keeps its shape, rhythm and comic build.

engine.meaning: It is the original nearly verbatim, so nothing is lost; "a pollie had been there" replaces the Congressman, keeping the joke.
engine.sense: The few terms fit: "that bloke that had that marvellous collection", "there is going to be heaps of it", "a pollie had been there".
engine.authenticity: What little Aussie there is sounds natural ("bloke", "heaps", "pollie"), but the US forms are left in all around it: "to-day's weather", "umbrella", "sally out", "Why, what awful thunder you have here!" "you are certain there is going to be heaps of it" is an odd join of formal and casual.
engine.register: It is largely untranslated. Only a handful of words change ("bloke", "heaps", "pollie", the spelling "favourable"), lighter even than level 1, let alone 2.
engine.tone: Twain's tone is fully intact because the text is: "you'll find that stranger down in the cellar with his head in the ash-barrel."
engine.flow: It reads as the original does; the only bump is "you are certain there is going to be heaps of it".
engine.variety: There's too little slang to repeat; each of the few swaps ("bloke", "heaps", "pollie") is used once.
engine.essence: It is unmistakably the original, since it is almost entirely the original.

yarn-dinkum.meaning: Every beat is kept, including the forecast and postscript verbatim. Additions are few, chiefly the opener "Here's one for ya." and "mate" in the quote. "patient, easygoing folk" softens forbearing slightly.
yarn-dinkum.sense: The terms fit: "knocked the foreigners for six", "blow-ins", "brolly", "a pollie had been through", "bumped up", "chews it over". "always minding its business" slightly shifts "attending strictly to business" (minding your own business means not interfering), a small strain.
yarn-dinkum.authenticity: It sounds like a real Australian telling it: "Dunno who makes that. My guess is", "crisp and confident as you like", "proud as punch", "Strewth, that's awful thunder you've got here!" Only the opener "Here's one for ya." feels stock.
yarn-dinkum.register: It is retold in a casual voice throughout, with idiom in most sentences ("knocked the foreigners for six", "proud as punch", "mucking about"). That's a bit heavier than level 2's moderate touch, but restrained, without piled-on tags.
yarn-dinkum.tone: The deadpan holds and the punchlines are left unexplained: "you'd reckon it was something valuable and a pollie had been through. And then there's the thunder."
yarn-dinkum.flow: It reads smoothly, with sensible paragraphs and natural rhythm: "Variety? He owned up he'd got hundreds of kinds of weather he'd never even heard of. And quantity?"
yarn-dinkum.variety: The slang and constructions are varied ("bumped up", "knocked the foreigners for six", "blow-ins", "proud as punch", "chews it over", "brolly", "Strewth"); "watch him" repeats but echoes the original.
yarn-dinkum.essence: It is plainly Twain's speech retold, with its shape and comic build intact.

unharnessed.meaning: It is close to the original throughout, but it rewrites the quoted forecast, which should stay the parody verbatim: "shifting to the southward", "points in between", "likely patches of rain". "samples from every climate" and "decent product" are fine paraphrases.
unharnessed.sense: Most terms fit ("blow-ins", "flabbergasted the foreigners", "knock off a lot of poets", "chucked away"), but "I reverently reckon" strains: reckon is casual opinion and clashes with reverently.
unharnessed.authenticity: It is mostly natural ("muck about and learn the trade", "hasn't got a clue", "Strewth, what awful thunder you've got here!"), but it keeps US forms: "a Congressman had been through" and "umbrella". "I reverently reckon" is a forced line.
unharnessed.register: A light, even touch at about level 2: "reckon", "muck about", "bloke", "flabbergasted", "blow-ins", "knock off", "Strewth". There's no swearing.
unharnessed.tone: The deadpan humour is intact and the punchline is left dry: "you'd think it was something valuable, and a Congressman had been through."
unharnessed.flow: It is generally smooth, in one long block. The opening "I reverently reckon" jars, and "reckon" twice in the first two sentences ("I reverently reckon" ... "but I reckon it must be") is clunky.
unharnessed.variety: "reckon" is doubled at the start; otherwise the swaps are varied ("flabbergasted", "blow-ins", "knock off", "chucked away", "Strewth").
unharnessed.essence: It is recognisably the original with its structure and jokes. Paraphrasing the parody forecast blunts one of its signature set pieces a little.

yarn-troppo.quote: a pollie had been through. Cleaned the place out.
yarn-troppo.original: you'd think it was something valuable, and a Congressman had been there.
yarn-troppo.why: Spelling out the joke flattens the dry, unfinished punchline.

yarn-troppo.quote: Now, ya might've heard this one.
yarn-troppo.why: A stock yarn opener bolted on; it pushes the register past level 2.

yarn-troppo.why: An added tag that weakens the climax of the list.

yarn-deadset.why: "muck about" suggests idle messing rather than trial and error.

yarn-deadset.quote: I reverently believe that the Maker who made us all makes everything in New England but the weather. I dunno who makes that
yarn-deadset.original: I reverently believe that the Maker who made us all makes everything in New England but the weather. I don't know who makes that
yarn-deadset.why: Formal Twain phrasing beside a casual "dunno" reads as patched.

engine.quote: And so the first thing they know the opportunity to inquire how they feel has permanently gone by.
engine.original: And so the first thing they know the opportunity to inquire how they feel has permanently gone by.
engine.why: Left untranslated, as is most of the text; far under a level-2 brief.

engine.quote: you are certain there is going to be heaps of it
engine.original: you are certain there is going to be plenty of it
engine.why: A lone slang word dropped into formal syntax.

yarn-dinkum.why: "Minding its business" reads as not interfering, near the opposite of the busy weather meant.

unharnessed.why: Reverently and reckon clash; an Australian would wince at the pairing.
A US form left in where "pollie" would localise the joke.

unharnessed.quote: likely patches of rain, snow, hail and drought
unharnessed.original: probable areas of rain, snow, hail, and drought
unharnessed.why: Rewrites the parody forecast, whose bureaucratic wording is the joke.

summaries.yarn-troppo: A lively, natural retelling that keeps every beat, but at a heavier weight than level 2, and its added punchlines sometimes explain the jokes.
summaries.yarn-deadset: A faithful light-touch rendering that sits right on level 2; the slang is natural, with a few patched joins against Twain's formal syntax.
summaries.engine: Essentially the original with three or four word swaps; it is faithful but well under the level-2 brief.
summaries.yarn-dinkum: A natural, faithful retelling that keeps the deadpan, slightly heavier than level 2 but well judged.
summaries.unharnessed: A light, level-appropriate rendering, marred by the clunky "reverently reckon", a leftover Congressman and a tampered forecast parody.
